passages.original: Interest tamen ut sciatur quemadmodum Tacitus imperator sit creatus, die VII kal. Octob. cum in Curiam Pompilianam ordo amplissimus consedisset, Velius Cornificius Gordianus consul dixit: Referemus ad vos, patres conscripti, quod saepe rettulimus ;
passages.english: It is worth knowing, however, how Tacitus was made emperor. On the seventh day before the Kalends of October, when the most distinguished order had taken their seats in the Curia Pompiliana, the consul Velius Cornificius Gordianus said: "We bring before you, conscript fathers, what we have often brought before you:
passages.notes: 'Curia Pompiliana' is the transmitted reading; the name of this senate-house is otherwise unclear. The consul's name is probably fictitious, as often in the Historia Augusta.

passages.original: nam et ipse auctor Aureliano fuisse perhibetur ut aurum a vestibus et cameris et pellibus summoveret, multa huius feruntur, sed longum est ea in litteras mittere, quod si quis omnia de hoc viro cupit scire, legat Suetonium Optatianum, qui eius vitam adfatim scripsit, legit sane senex minutulas litteras ad stuporem nec umquam noctem intermisit qua non aliquid vel scriberet ille vel legeret praeter posterum kalendarum diem.
passages.english: For he himself is also said to have been the one who urged Aurelian to remove gold from garments, ceilings and leather hangings. Many [sayings] of his are reported, but it would take long to commit them to writing. But if anyone wishes to know everything about this man, let him read Suetonius Optatianus, who wrote his life in full. Indeed, as an old man he read very small letters to [the point of] astonishment, and he never let a night pass in which he did not either write or read something, except the day after the Kalends.
passages.notes: 'pellibus' (skins, leather hangings) is uncertain in sense; some editors suspect corruption. Suetonius Optatianus is otherwise unknown and probably invented. 'praeter posterum kalendarum diem' is obscure: possibly the day after the Kalends was regarded as ill-omened.

passages.original: et quoniam a Maeotide multi barbari eruperant, hos eosdem consilio atque virtute compressit. ipsi autem Maeotidae ita se gregabant, quasi accitu Aureliani ad bellum Persicum convenissent, auxilium daturi nostris si necessitas postularet. M. Tullius dicit magnificentius esse dicere, quemadmodum gesserit quam quemadmodum ceperit consulatum ; at in isto viro magnificum fuit quod tanta gloria cepit imperium; gessit autem propter brevitatem temporum nihil magnum, interemptus est enim insidiis militaribus, ut alii dicunt, sexto mense, ut alii, morbo interiit, tamen constat factionibus eum oppressum mente atque animo defecisse, hic idem mensem Septembrem Tacitum appellari iussit, idcirco quod eo mense et natus et factus est imperator.
passages.english: And since many barbarians had broken out from the Maeotis, he crushed these same [barbarians] by strategy and courage. The Maeotidae themselves, however, were gathering in bands as though they had assembled at Aurelian's summons for the Persian war, to give help to our men if need required. Marcus Tullius says that it is more splendid to speak of how one conducted the consulship than of how one obtained it. But in this man the splendid thing was that he obtained the empire with such great glory; yet because of the shortness of his time he accomplished nothing great. For he was killed by a military plot, as some say, in the sixth month; as others [say], he died of illness. It is agreed, however, that, overwhelmed by factions, he failed in mind and spirit. This same man ordered the month of September to be called Tacitus, because in that month he was both born and made emperor.
passages.notes: Maeotis is the Sea of Azov region. The 'Maeotidae' passage is awkwardly phrased; the sense seems to be that the barbarians pretended to have gathered as Roman allies.
